challenges.headline: Build versus configure existing circuit
challenges.premise: Manager approval with escalation is a new feature to build.
challenges.alternative: The platform already has absence management and shared approval circuits. It is possible that manager approval already works and only the escalation rule is missing, which would turn this into a configuration or a small extension rather than a new flow.
challenges.consequence: Building a parallel approval flow would duplicate logic that other modules share, and risk diverging from the existing permission and notification behaviour.
challenges.recommendation: Review how leave is approved today and where it fails, then size only the gap before committing to any build.

challenges.headline: Undefined meaning of 'away'
challenges.premise: The system can tell when a manager is away and escalate accordingly.
challenges.alternative: Escalation can be triggered by a declared absence or delegate, or by a simple timeout with no reply after N days. A timeout needs no availability data and also covers a manager who is present but not responding.
challenges.consequence: A status-based trigger depends on absence data being accurate and may miss unresponsive managers. A timeout adds scheduled processing and a waiting period. Each is a different build.
challenges.recommendation: Decide with the client whether away means approved leave, a delegate, or a timeout, and who takes over, before estimating.

challenges.headline: Approval hides balance checks
challenges.premise: Approval is a simple manager yes/no decision.
challenges.alternative: Leave approval on this platform commonly includes a balance or quota check (paid leave, RTT) and sometimes a second level. Settling whether the check happens at submission, at approval, or at escalation keeps the escalation step from approving leave the employee cannot take.
challenges.consequence: If escalation bypasses the balance check, or if balances change while a request is pending, approvals can be wrong and hard to unwind under French labor-law rules.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm the scope of the decision step, including balance checks and leave types, before designing the workflow.

If per-client configuration is needed late, the escalation rule hardcoded early will have to be reworked.

challenges.premise: Manager approval with escalation is a new feature to build.

challenges.recommendation: Before any estimate, inspect what the current absence approval circuit supports (manager step, delegation, escalation) and which of it is switched off or unused.

challenges.headline: What 'away' actually means
challenges.premise: Escalation fires when the manager is away, as if that were a single, detectable state.
challenges.alternative: Three different triggers exist: the manager's own approved leave or a declared absence, a delegate the manager names in advance, or no response after a set number of days. A timeout is the only one that needs no one to maintain a status, and it also covers a manager who is present but unresponsive. It can be combined with the others later.
challenges.consequence: A status-based trigger relies on managers keeping their absence up to date, and requests still stall when they forget. A timer-based trigger needs a delay value, reminders and a decision on whether the original manager can still act after escalation. Choosing wrongly means rebuilding the workflow core.
challenges.recommendation: Get the client to pick the trigger, and the escalation target (manager's manager, delegate or HR), before design. This is a proposal to validate, not a settled choice.

challenges.headline: Approval as a simple yes/no
challenges.premise: A manager approves or rejects a request, and the escalation merely changes who does it.
challenges.alternative: On this platform, approval typically also involves a leave balance or quota check and possibly several levels. Treating the escalation approver as a full substitute at every level, or stating explicitly that balance validation sits outside this scope, keeps the circuit coherent.
challenges.consequence: If balance checks and multi-level steps surface during build, the escalation design has to be reworked, and French paid leave and RTT rules can vary by client and leave type.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm whether balance validation and multiple levels are in scope, and whether the rules vary by client, country or leave type.

challenges.headline: Undefined meaning of 'away'
challenges.premise: The system can tell when a manager is away and reroute the request at that moment.
challenges.alternative: A timeout-based escalation (reminder after N days, then escalate) needs no knowledge of absence data, whereas a declared-absence trigger requires a reliable absence calendar. A manager-set delegate in advance is a third, simpler option. These are my proposals, not the client's choice.
challenges.consequence: Each reading of 'away' implies a different build. Detecting absence from the leave calendar creates a dependency on the manager's own leave data being accurate and complete, and a request can still stall if the manager is simply unresponsive.
challenges.recommendation: Have the client choose the trigger explicitly. Consider timeout plus optional delegation as the lowest-dependency starting point.

challenges.headline: Approval without a balance check
challenges.premise: Approval is a manager's yes or no decision on the request.
challenges.alternative: Treat approval as a decision supported by a balance and quota check, so the approver sees whether the employee has enough paid leave or RTT before deciding. Whether this applies is unconfirmed.
challenges.consequence: If the balance check is expected but left out, managers (and escalation approvers) can approve leave the employee cannot take, creating French labor-law and payroll corrections after the fact.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm whether balance validation belongs in this scope, and whether rules differ by leave type or country, before fixing the workflow.

complexity_reasons: shared approval circuit and permissions affect other modules
escalation trigger and target still undefined
possible per-client configurability on a multi-client platform
edge cases such as no manager, manager as requester and manager returning after escalation
briefs.cost_driver: the escalation trigger and whether it must be configurable per client
risks: Changing the shared approval circuit or permission rules may alter behaviour on other screens and modules.
Requests already in flight at rollout need a defined handling path, or they could be stranded or double-decided.
Escalation without a defined end state can produce duplicate or conflicting decisions when the original manager returns.
Escalation gives a second person access to HR data, which raises GDPR and permission-scoping exposure.
Permissions are likely to be discovered late, at acceptance testing, if not specified up front.

opportunities.text: Make escalation and delegation a reusable capability of the shared approval circuit rather than a leave-only feature.
Record every approval, escalation and decision in a common history that HR can consult.
Route notifications by the contact or approver role so the same routing serves other approval flows.

next_steps: Establish how leave is approved today and whether the shared approval circuit already supports delegation or multi-level steps.
Get the client to decide the escalation trigger (declared absence, advance delegate or timeout), the target approver, and whether a balance check is part of approval.
Confirm whether the rule is the same for all clients or configurable, then estimate the build on that basis.
Define the edge-case outcomes (no manager, manager is requester, manager returns after escalation) and the acceptance scenarios before starting.
open_decisions: Escalation trigger: declared absence, advance delegate or timeout
Escalation target: manager's manager, HR or a named delegate
Whether approval includes a balance or quota check, and whether rules vary by leave type or country
Whether the rule is common to all clients or configurable per client
Who is notified, on which event and through which channel
How HR is involved (visibility, override rights)
Success measures, for example maximum time a request may stay pending
Audit and history expectations for decisions and escalations
Handling of in-flight requests at rollout and of the edge cases
